title: Stroke & other emergencies
blurb: Use FAST to spot a stroke and call 999, calm a hyperventilating patient, and recognise local anaesthetic toxicity.
question: While the dentist writes up the notes, an elderly patient tries to answer a question but her words come out slurred. The left side of her mouth has dropped and she can't lift her left arm. What is happening, what do you do, and why does the time matter?

teach.body: A stroke happens when the blood supply to part of the brain is cut off, either by a clot blocking an artery or by a bleed. Brain cells start dying within minutes, so every minute counts: the sooner hospital treatment starts, the more brain can be saved. Signs come on suddenly and usually affect one side of the body. A transient ischaemic attack (TIA, or 'mini-stroke') causes the same signs but they clear up. It is a warning and still needs urgent assessment.

letters.sub: Has one side drooped? Can they smile?
Can they raise both arms and keep them up?
Is it slurred, garbled or missing?
Time to call 999. Note when it started.

steps.label: Call 999 immediately
steps.sub: Say 'suspected stroke'; note the time it began

steps.label: Reassure and monitor ABCDE
steps.sub: Glucose check if trained: a hypo can mimic a stroke

steps.label: Unconscious but breathing
steps.sub: Recovery position; CPR if not breathing normally

teach.body: An anxious patient may breathe too fast and too deeply, blowing off too much carbon dioxide. Signs: rapid breathing, light-headedness, tingling in the fingers and around the mouth, a tight chest, palpitations and sometimes cramping of the hands. Stop treatment, reassure calmly and coach slow breathing ('breathe in with me… and out'). Breathing into a paper bag is no longer recommended. First make sure it isn't something more serious, such as asthma, anaphylaxis, a hypo or a heart problem.

If too much local anaesthetic reaches the bloodstream, usually from too large a dose or accidental injection into a blood vessel, it affects the brain and heart. This is why the dentist aspirates before injecting. Early signs: ringing in the ears (tinnitus), a metallic taste, light-headedness, restlessness and agitation, slurred speech and drowsiness. It can progress to seizures, unconsciousness, heart rhythm problems and cardiac arrest. Stop, call for help, assess ABCDE, give oxygen and call 999 if it worsens.

rows.label: Key signs
values: Face droop, arm weakness, slurred speech

teach.h: Unwell soon after an LA injection?
teach.caption: A faint is by far the most likely, but always look for the signs that point elsewhere.

teach.text: Don't hold off calling 999 because stroke signs are improving: a TIA still needs urgent assessment. And don't reach for a paper bag for hyperventilation; coach slow breathing instead.

items: Stroke: sudden face droop, arm weakness or slurred speech, usually one-sided.
FAST: Face, Arms, Speech, Time to call 999. Note the time the signs started.
Stroke: nothing by mouth, monitor ABCDE, recovery position if unconscious and breathing.
Hyperventilation: fast breathing, tingling, dizziness; reassure and coach slow breathing.
LA toxicity: tinnitus, metallic taste, restlessness; can lead to seizures and cardiac arrest.

summary: You can now use FAST to recognise a stroke and act fast, manage a suspected stroke safely until the ambulance arrives, calm a hyperventilating patient without a paper bag, and recognise the early signs of local anaesthetic toxicity.

A.q: A patient's face suddenly droops on one side, her speech is slurred and she can't lift one arm. What is the most likely cause?
A.why: Sudden one-sided facial droop, arm weakness and slurred speech are the FAST signs of a stroke.

whyNot.0: A faint causes brief loss of consciousness with quick recovery, not one-sided weakness.
whyNot.1: Hyperventilation causes fast breathing and tingling, not facial droop or arm weakness.
whyNot.2: A hypo can mimic some signs, but one-sided FAST signs strongly suggest a stroke.

A.q: In the FAST stroke check, what does the 'T' stand for?
A.why: T is Time: time to call 999, and note the time the signs started.

whyNot.0: Aspirin isn't given in suspected stroke because it could worsen a bleed.
whyNot.2: A glucose check can help rule out a hypo, but it isn't the T in FAST.
whyNot.3: Chair position isn't part of the FAST check.

A.q: An anxious patient is breathing fast and says her fingers are tingling. Asthma and anaphylaxis have been ruled out. What should you do?
options: Give her a paper bag to breathe into
Lay her flat and raise her legs
A.why: Reassurance and coaching slow, calm breathing settle hyperventilation once serious causes are excluded.

whyNot.0: Paper bag rebreathing is no longer recommended.
whyNot.2: Adrenaline is for anaphylaxis, not anxiety-driven over-breathing.
whyNot.3: Lying flat with legs raised is the treatment for a faint.

B.q: Shortly after an LA injection, a patient complains of ringing in his ears and a metallic taste, and becomes restless. What do these signs suggest?
B.why: Tinnitus, a metallic taste and restlessness after an injection are early signs of local anaesthetic toxicity.

whyNot.0: Allergy causes rash, swelling, wheeze or collapse, not tinnitus or a metallic taste.
whyNot.1: A faint causes pallor, sweating and dizziness.

B.q: Why shouldn't a patient with a suspected stroke be given anything to eat or drink?
B.why: A stroke can weaken the swallowing muscles, so food or drink could go into the lungs.

whyNot.1: Eating or drinking doesn't meaningfully raise blood pressure.
whyNot.2: Food or drink doesn't mask FAST signs.
whyNot.3: Food and drink don't thin the blood.

B.q: Which group of signs suggests hyperventilation?
options: Face droop, slurred speech, weak arm
B.why: Rapid breathing with tingling fingers in an anxious patient is typical of hyperventilation.

whyNot.0: Wheeze with swelling and rash suggests anaphylaxis.
whyNot.2: Face droop, slurred speech and arm weakness suggest a stroke.
whyNot.3: Crushing chest pain with clamminess suggests a heart attack.

C.q: A patient's facial droop and slurred speech clear up within ten minutes. What should happen?
options: Nothing, as the signs have gone
Book a GP visit next month
C.why: Signs that resolve may be a TIA, a warning of a possible stroke, which still needs urgent medical assessment.

whyNot.0: A TIA is a warning sign and must not be ignored.
whyNot.1: A TIA needs urgent assessment, not a routine appointment.
whyNot.3: Aspirin isn't given by the dental team in suspected stroke, and the patient needs assessment.

C.q: What is a common cause of local anaesthetic toxicity?
options: An allergy to latex in the gloves
C.why: Accidental injection into a blood vessel (or too large a dose) puts too much LA into the bloodstream. Aspirating first helps prevent this.

whyNot.1: Latex allergy causes an allergic reaction, not LA toxicity.
whyNot.2: Topical anaesthetic before injection doesn't cause toxicity in normal use.
whyNot.3: Needle length doesn't by itself cause toxicity.

C.q: Which is NOT one of the FAST stroke checks?
C.why: FAST checks Face, Arms and Speech, then Time to call 999. Temperature isn't part of it.

whyNot.0: Face droop is the F in FAST.
whyNot.1: Arm weakness is the A in FAST.
whyNot.2: Slurred speech is the S in FAST.

reteach.title: A blocked road and a ticking clock
reteach.question: Think of the brain as a town and its arteries as roads. What happens when a road is blocked, and why does the ambulance need to know the exact time?

blocks.body: When a road into part of the brain is blocked or bursts, the neighbourhood beyond it loses its supplies and starts to shut down: a drooping face, a weak arm, jumbled speech. Hospital teams can sometimes clear the road, but only within a limited time from when it started. That's why the T in FAST matters twice: call 999 now, and tell them exactly when the signs began.

items.label: Notice FAST signs; note the time
Nothing by mouth, reassure, monitor ABCDE
Tell paramedics the time it started

explain.body: Face: one side drooping? Arms: can they lift both? Speech: slurred or garbled? Time: call 999 and note when it started.

test.q: You ask a patient to raise both arms and one drifts down. Which part of FAST is this testing?
test.why: A is for Arms: weakness or drift in one arm is a stroke sign.

whyNot.0: Face checks for drooping on one side.
whyNot.1: Speech checks for slurred or garbled words.

explain.body: Call 999, note the time, give nothing by mouth, reassure and monitor ABCDE. Recovery position if unconscious and breathing; CPR if not breathing normally.

test.q: A conscious patient with suspected stroke is breathing normally. What is the best management while waiting?
options: Walk them to the car park
test.why: Stay with the patient, reassure them, give nothing by mouth and monitor ABCDE until the ambulance arrives.

whyNot.0: A stroke patient shouldn't walk or be moved unnecessarily.
whyNot.2: Nothing should be given by mouth because swallowing may be affected.
whyNot.3: The patient may deteriorate and must not be left alone.

explain.body: Over-breathing from anxiety lowers carbon dioxide: fast breathing, dizziness, tingling fingers and lips. Rule out serious causes, then reassure and coach slow breathing. No paper bag.

test.q: Why is breathing into a paper bag no longer recommended for hyperventilation?
test.why: Rebreathing can lower oxygen levels and may hide a more serious cause of fast breathing.

whyNot.1: Tingling comes from low carbon dioxide; that isn't the reason for avoiding the bag.
whyNot.2: Heart rate isn't the main concern.
whyNot.3: Causing a faint isn't the reason it's avoided.

explain.body: Too much LA in the blood (large dose or injection into a vessel). Early: tinnitus, metallic taste, light-headedness, restlessness. Later: seizures, unconsciousness, cardiac arrest. Stop, ABCDE, oxygen, 999 if worsening.

test.q: Which sign after an LA injection points to toxicity rather than an allergic reaction?
test.why: Tinnitus is an early sign of LA toxicity. Rash, swelling and wheeze point to allergy.

whyNot.0: A rash suggests an allergic reaction.
whyNot.1: Lip swelling suggests an allergic reaction.
